Furthermore, we prove the equivalence of the notion of viscosity-variational inequality solution with the notion of a partial differential inclusion solution, where the value function is a strong solution of the HJB equation and the player density is a very weak solution of the KFP equation with coefficients belonging to subdifferential sets of the Hamiltonian. Finally, we prove the uniqueness of solutions in the case of separable Hamiltonians with strictly monotone couplings.

item.title: All minimum cuts of symmetric submodular functions
item.description: We compute Cunningham's canonical decomposition of a symmetric submodular function on $n$ elements in $O(n^3)$ time. The decomposition represents all minimum cuts in linear space. For the pair $s,t$ produced by Queyranne's algorithm, we construct in $O(n^2)$ time a digraph representing exactly the minimum $st$-cuts of the function. Using this construction in Chekuri and Xu's decomposition algorithm gives the cubic bound.

item.title: A Proximal Newton Framework with Local Superlinear Convergence for Simple Bilevel Optimization
item.description: In this paper, we study a penalty method for simple bilevel optimization in which the lower-level objective has a convex composite structure. Our approach is based on a vanishing-penalty reformulation, which gives rise to a sequence of penalized problems as the penalty parameter decreases. A key difficulty is that metric subregularity of the lower-level optimality mapping does not, in general, yield a uniform error bound for the penalized problems as the penalty parameter vanishes, preventing a direct application of standard proximal Newton theory. To address this difficulty, we first analyze a regularized proximal Newton step by exploiting the specific structure of simple bilevel problems, and establish the local estimates that underpin superlinear convergence. Building on this local analysis, we propose SiB-Newton, which incorporates the proximal Newton step into a globalization strategy. We establish convergence guarantees for SiB-Newton and show that, under suitable local conditions, Newton steps are eventually accepted and the iterates converge at a superlinear rate. Numerical experiments on synthetic examples verify the predicted local superlinear convergence rate.

item.title: Dynamic Optimistic Constrained OCO with Memory via Delay Equivalence
item.description: Online Convex Optimization with memory and time-varying constraints (COCO-M) is a recently-introduced framework that captures the dynamics of stateful online learning and non-stochastic control with budget constraints. Despite its expressive power, COCO-M remains largely understudied. In this work, we tackle this problem in its full scale, providing an optimistic algorithm that incorporates untrusted predictions to tame universal dynamic regret and cumulative constraint violation. Our analysis leverages a potent reduction from memory to delay and treats state-dependent gradients as delayed feedback. We establish the first bounds that adapt to both environment non-stationarity (path length $P_T$) and prediction accuracy, while lifting previous restrictive assumptions such as functional separability. En route to these results, we derive findings of independent interest for the memory-to-delay reduction, and for delayed OCO with time-varying constraints. The proposed framework ensures sublinear worst-case guarantees that improve with prediction accuracy, reaching $\mathcal O(1)$ regret under perfect predictions, with cumulative constraint violation (CCV) $\mathcal O(\sqrt{T})$ for unknown $P_T$ and $\mathcal O(\log T)$ for known or online observable $P_T$ , while recovering the optimal COCO rates when memory disappears.

item.title: Hardness of integer linear feasibility with cyclic support
item.description: We prove that integer linear feasibility is strongly $NP$-complete even when the constraint matrix has exactly two nonzero entries in every row and column, with its support forming a single cycle. This holds already for monotone systems (one positive and one negative coefficient in each inequality) with nonzero coefficients of absolute value $2$ or $3$ and right-hand sides in $\{-1,0,1,2\}$. No variable bounds are supplied separately from the system. For systems in which each inequality involves at most two variables, this strengthens known hardness results by restricting all numerical data to fixed finite sets. For systems in which each variable occurs in at most two inequalities, this establishes, to the best of our knowledge, the first $NP$-hardness result for feasibility. We also give negative answers, unless $P=NP$, to questions on polynomial-time solvability of integer programs with bounded coefficients and bounded totally $Δ$-modular treewidth, and on fixed-parameter tractability of integer bound propagation with respect to coefficient and right-hand-side magnitudes.

item.title: A Theoretical Analysis of a Bilevel Optimization Formulation for Combined Local-Global Optical Flow Models
item.description: This paper analyzes a bilevel formulation for learning the regularization parameter of combined local-global (CLG) optical flow models. The lower-level problem computes the flow from a Lucas--Kanade data term and a quadratic or total variation (TV) regularizer, and the upper-level problem selects the parameter that minimizes the squared distance to a ground-truth flow. The setting is finite-dimensional, and a full-rank assumption makes the lower-level solution unique. For the quadratic model we derive sufficient conditions for the existence of an optimal parameter, for every optimal parameter to be positive, and for strict local optimality. For TV regularization an optimal parameter always exists, because the lower-level solution vanishes for large parameters, and we give a sufficient condition for positivity that accounts for the coupling of the two flow components through the local structure tensors. Synthetic examples illustrate the conditions, including cases in which they fail.

item.title: Augmented Lagrangian methods with telescopic subproblems for MPCCs and cardinality constraints with general constraints: constraint-preserving swaps and B-stationarity
item.description: We consider optimization problems with general equality and inequality constraints and partitioned cardinality constraints, which include complementarity constraints. In the augmented Lagrangian method that we consider, the bounds and the cardinality constraints are kept in the subproblems, which are solved by the Telescopic Method. The limit points of this method are B-stationary, without constraint qualifications, if the penalty parameters remain bounded, but not in general. The reason is that the swaps of the Telescopic Method pass through points at which the constraints have different values, and the corresponding variation of the penalty term grows with the penalty parameter. With unbounded penalty parameters and a derivative test outside the current face, the feasible limit points at which a linear independence constraint qualification holds are M-stationary for MPCCs. We modify the swaps, by means of a scaled Newton restoration, so that they preserve the values of the constraints, and we prove that every feasible limit point at which this constraint qualification holds is then B-stationary (S-stationary for MPCCs), whatever the behavior of the penalty parameters. Counterexamples show that the modification is necessary, even with exact solutions of the subproblems, and that the constraint qualification cannot be weakened to one of Mangasarian-Fromovitz type. In the MacMPEC collection, the method found certified S- or B-stationary points in 185 of the 193 instances, more than Algencan and the regularization method of Scholtes. In experiments with cardinality-constrained portfolios and sparse principal component analysis, the constraint-preserving swaps improved the original swaps and the methods applied to complementarity reformulations.

item.title: Adversarial Training with Large Step Sizes: Implicit Bias, Optimization, and Sharpness
item.description: Adversarial Training (AT) is an important method for improving model robustness. We study the dynamics of deterministic Gradient Descent (GD) in AT. Most existing works in this direction focus on the small or vanishing step sizes regime, where GD resembles a continuous-time flow. However, such step sizes can make training inefficient and are rarely used in practice. In this paper, we study the AT dynamics of GD with large constant step sizes. We first study GD in adversarial linear logistic regression, focusing on two aspects: where the model parameters converge (implicit bias) and how quickly the losses decrease (optimization). We then turn to neural networks training and study how the sharpness of losses evolve during AT. Our results advance the understanding of the behaviors of GD with large step sizes in AT and highlight three key differences from its behavior in Standard Training (ST): (i) the implicit bias gap between AT and ST, previously established only for small step sizes, persists for arbitrarily large constant step sizes, (ii) different from ST, there is no uniform rate of convergence for the optimization error in AT, and (iii) sharpness can exhibit two-stage dynamics that differ from the Edge-of-Stability behavior observed in ST.

item.title: An Accelerated Proximal Gradient Method for Bures-Wasserstein Space
item.description: We study composite optimization over the Bures--Wasserstein (BW) space of Gaussian measures. Our main observation is that a useful class of BW problems can be lifted into the Euclidean space of affine transport maps, such that the lifted problems can be solved efficiently using accelerated proximal gradient methods. For objectives whose smooth and nonsmooth components admit convex smooth and convex proximable affine lifts, respectively, our algorithm BW-FISTA achieves minimax-optimal objective gap $O(k^{-2})$ after $k$ iterations. We verify these regularity conditions for potential and interaction energies together with common spectral regularizers, and we treat stochastic gradients under a suitable noise model. As a principal application, we consider Gaussian variational inference with a log-concave, log-smooth target. Here, the resulting entropy term is handled by an efficient, exact proximal step, and we improve the previous rate of $O(k^{-1})$ to $O(k^{-2})$. We numerically verify this predicted boost with synthetic experiments.

item.title: Model-based learning for DoA estimation and array calibration via continuous sparse recovery
item.description: Direction of arrival (DoA) estimation, a classical signal processing problem, has experienced renewed interest with the advent of integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). While decades of research have yielded highly accurate DoA estimators, hardware impairments have frequently been neglected, despite degrading both DoA estimation accuracy and downstream communication performance in ISAC systems. This work introduces a joint array calibration and DoA estimation method based on the simultaneous orthogonal matching pursuit (SOMP) algorithm, following the model-based machine learning paradigm. The proposed method enables the calibration of antenna arrays subject to severe gain-phase and antenna location impairments through projected gradient descent (PGD), with either supervised or unsupervised objectives. Additionally, DoA estimation is enhanced by extending SOMP to continuous dictionaries via PGD refinement steps. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method enables efficient hardware impairment compensation, even without labeled samples, while outperforming conventional sparse recovery and subspace-based DoA estimation baselines.

item.title: Coordinatewise Epsilon for Adam under Heavy-Tailed Noise
item.description: Adam estimates second moments coordinatewise, but typically adds the same scalar $\varepsilon$ to every denominator. We study how this shared $\varepsilon$ affects convergence when noise and curvature vary across coordinates. Under coordinatewise finite-$p$ noise moments, $p\in(1,2]$, choosing $\varepsilon_i$ from the noise and curvature bounds for each coordinate attains the heavy-tailed $\ell_1$-stationarity benchmark $O(T^{-\frac{p-1}{3p-2}})$, matching the known optimal time exponent for smooth nonconvex stochastic optimization. For $1<p<2$, Adam with a shared $\varepsilon_t$ admits a lower bound of order $Ω(T^{-\frac{p-1}{2p}})$. This lower bound holds for every predictable scalar choice of $η_t$, $β_{1,t}$, $β_{2,t}$, and $\varepsilon_t$, precluding a dimension-uniform benchmark rate for this class.

item.title: Encoding Memory in World Models with Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
item.description: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning. In this work, we address the problem of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. We introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode observations into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark. Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.

item.title: Spiking neuromodulation: a linear control perspective
item.description: Neuronal excitability is a nonlinear phenomenon, and the complexity of spiking experimental traces sometimes looks defeating. The present paper takes the view point that excitability is a neuromodulated property, and aims to demonstrate that the neuromodulation of spiking is amenable to the classical linear analysis tools of control theory. We illustrate the value of linear feedback analysis as an alternative to bifurcation analysis in the simple yet classical example of spiking modulation by the A-type potassium current.

item.title: Branch-Extended Automatic Differentiation
item.description: We present branch-extended automatic differentiation (BEAD), a software package that provides information about inactive branches of piecewise-differentiable functions, intended for use in nonsmooth optimization algorithms. BEAD is implemented in Python, building on the popular JAX framework. For supported nonsmooth operations such as abs and max, BEAD identifies alternative branches within tolerance from the given input, and computes gradients of the resulting branches extended to the given input. Such information has been previously used for robust optimization methods, but has required error-prone and tedious manual differentiation, unlike BEAD, which is fully automated for functions written in NumPy-like JAX code. Our experiments show that our approach is as accurate as manually written derivative code, and offers more flexibility in modifying the function and choosing between branch-discovery rules. While we were originally motivated by the manifold sampling algorithm for nonsmooth composite objectives, we also integrate BEAD branch-extension gradients into a nonsmooth BFGS-SQP solver. On two small nonsmooth test problems, the resulting path-aware search resolves failures or substantially reduces the number of evaluations required by the BFGS-SQP solver.

item.title: Compressed Per-Player Local Methods for Multiplayer Federated Learning: Exact Convergence via Increment Sharing
item.description: Multiplayer Federated Learning (MpFL), introduced by Yoon et al. (2025), extends classical federated learning to settings where clients are rational players in a game with individual objectives and strategies, seeking an equilibrium. A natural baseline is Per-Player Local SGD (PEARL-SGD), where each player performs several local SGD steps before exchanging strategies through a central server. However, the original PEARL-SGD formulation does not extend cleanly to compressed communication. Directly compressing the players' strategies can prevent convergence to the equilibrium, even with deterministic gradients. To address this issue, we reformulate PEARL-SGD so that players communicate local strategy increments rather than the strategies themselves. Without compression, the two formulations are equivalent, but with compression, increment sharing preserves exact convergence, allowing us to design the communication-efficient compressed PEARL-SGD (C-PEARL-SGD). Beyond compression, we also consider variance reduction as another axis of improvement, introducing PEARL-SVRG and its compressed variant C-PEARL-SVRG. Under the original MpFL assumptions, we establish convergence guarantees for all variants through a unified parametric inequality. Numerical experiments, including distributed spectrum sensing, demonstrate the practical benefits of our methods over vanilla PEARL-SGD.

item.title: Optimal Feedback Control of the Fokker-Planck Equation for an SIRS Epidemic Model
item.description: We develop a Fokker--Planck feedback control framework for a stochastic susceptible--infected--recovered--susceptible (SIRS) epidemic model with three intervention mechanisms targeting disease transmission, loss of immunity, and recovery. The interventions are formulated as space- and time-dependent feedback controls that influence both the drift and diffusion coefficients of the underlying stochastic differential equations, allowing control of the probability distribution of epidemic states. We investigate the existence of optimal controls and derive first-order necessary optimality conditions involving a forward Fokker--Planck equation, a backward adjoint equation, and a Hamiltonian minimization condition. For numerical approximation, we combine a Chang--Cooper discretization of the diagonal drift--diffusion terms with a finite-difference treatment of cross-diffusion and a sequential quadratic Hamiltonian (SQH) algorithm for computing the optimal feedback policies. We also examine sufficient-decrease and convergence properties of the SQH iteration. Numerical experiments consider four epidemiological objectives involving cumulative infection burden, infection-threshold exceedance, terminal susceptible population, and a combination of running and terminal costs. The resulting feedback policies exhibit distinct spatial and temporal structures depending on the epidemiological objective. Monte Carlo simulations of the underlying stochastic system illustrate that the optimized interventions can substantially reduce infection growth and undesirable epidemic outcomes relative to uncontrolled dynamics. The proposed framework provides a distribution-based approach to stochastic epidemic control that integrates mathematical analysis, numerical optimization, and state-dependent intervention design.

item.title: Vector Lyapunov functions for nonconvex constrained optimization
item.description: Nonconvex constrained optimization problems are commonly solved by a Newton method for necessary conditions (sequential linear/quadratic programming) or a barrier reformulation (interior-point methods). We present a vector Lyapunov analysis for Newton-type algorithms based on constraint violation and optimality of the primal solutions to a sequence of approximate optimization problems. We thus prove local stability and convergence by constructing a strict Lyapunov function for the primal solution.

item.title: Entropic Martingale Optimal Transport with Wasserstein Relaxed Marginal Constraints
item.description: Martingale optimal transport (MOT) is a fundamental framework in robust finance, yet its stability under marginal perturbation no longer holds in high dimensions $d\geq 2$. In this paper, we introduce Wasserstein-relaxed entropic martingale optimal transport (WEMOT), which combines Wasserstein relaxation of the second marginal with entropy regularization. This formulation ensures stability under perturbations of the marginals, thereby facilitating numerical implementation. We establish strong duality and dual attainment for WEMOT, which leads to efficient Sinkhorn-type algorithms. We further prove a convergence rate of WEMOT to MOT as regularization parameters vanish, and also the quantitative stability of WEMOT with respect to marginal perturbations.

item.title: On Lipschitz Explosion in Deep Neural Networks with Normalization: Consequences for Optimization and Adversarial Robustness
item.description: Can a network look stable at every layer and still be exponentially unstable as a whole? The Lipschitz constant of a neural network is a basic stability quantity appearing in optimization guarantees, generalization bounds, and robustness certificates. Deep networks naturally admit two such notions, input Lipschitzness, measuring sensitivity to data perturbations, and parameter Lipschitzness, measuring sensitivity to weight perturbations. We prove that, for deep networks with normalization layers, with batch normalization as the canonical example, both Lipschitz constants can grow exponentially with depth and hence with parameter dimension, even under strong per-layer norm control such as $\|W_\ell\|_2\le 1$, and already for linear activations. Thus, a mechanism widely used to stabilize training can create severe worst-case instabilities that are invisible locally, i.e., from layerwise norm bounds alone. Parameter-Lipschitz explosion turns Lipschitz-dependent nonsmooth optimization guarantees into exponential-in-dimension bounds for deep normalized networks, while input-Lipschitz explosion makes worst-case Lipschitz-based generalization and robustness certificates vacuous. The latter also yields a concrete rank-separation mechanism for adversarial vulnerability. The theory predicts that perturbations introducing new singular directions should be amplified much more strongly than perturbations at the same noise level that remain within the input's original singular subspace. Experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 support this prediction, showing that rank-creating perturbations cause substantially sharper drops in accuracy, confidence, and margins than same-subspace perturbations.

item.title: Synchronized Optimal Transport Reconstructs Coupled Transcriptomic and Chromatin Dynamics
item.description: Single-cell RNA and ATAC data collected across developmental stages provide time-course snapshots of transcriptional and regulatory states. Since sequencing is destructive, trajectories between these snapshots must be inferred from independently sampled cell populations. Existing approaches typically infer continuous dynamics in a single modality or integrate RNA and ATAC in a shared representation. Here we present Cross-Omics Aligned Trajectory Inference (COATI), which extends unbalanced synchronized dynamical optimal transport to time-dependent cross-modal maps for reconstructing coupled trajectories in distinct RNA and ATAC state spaces. We evaluated COATI on synthetic benchmarks and four developmental datasets using held-out-stage reconstruction and lineage analyses. COATI improved reconstruction of cell populations at held-out stages, including recovery of chromatin-state heterogeneity within cell types, and better preserved developmental lineage relationships. The unbalanced formulation allows the inference of population mass changes, which were shown to associate with DNA-replication programs at early stages and lineage-maturation programs later in development. The coupled trajectories enabled analysis of lineage-specific transcriptional and chromatin changes and their temporal relationships during development. Lineage responses inferred by COATI agreed with independent CRISPR perturbation results, and the inferred regulatory patterns were consistent with independent epigenetic data.

item.title: Supporting Data Center Grid Integration via Co-Optimized Battery Energy Storage Sizing and Capacity Allocation
item.description: Interconnecting large data centers can be delayed by grid requirements on demand flexibility, ramping limits, and ride-through performance. This paper proposes an optimization-based framework to size a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) that accelerates data center grid integration by providing BESS capacity required to meet selected flexibility and grid-support requirements. The model co-optimizes BESS power rating and energy capacity while allocating capability across three services: (i) demand response over a specified duration, (ii) mitigation of high-magnitude, high-frequency load fluctuations through reserved active power with zero net state-of-charge change, and (iii) voltage support via reactive power capability at the point of common coupling. Minute-level operational scheduling enforces state-of-charge feasibility and load ramp constraints, and incorporates a controllable queue of delay-insensitive computing tasks to enhance flexibility. A case study using a real data center load profile demonstrates the proposed method and quantifies the BESS power-energy requirements and operational trade-offs needed to satisfy the multi-service constraints, providing practical guidance for interconnection planning and deployment.

item.title: Constrained Nested-Logit Pricing: An Exact Reformulation and Global Optimization Method
item.description: Sellers must price substitutable products while meeting operational requirements such as price limits and sales targets. Nested logit captures stronger substitution among similar products, but these requirements can undermine the structure used to solve unconstrained pricing problems. We develop an exact reformulation and a global optimization method for a fixed assortment with price bounds and weighted price caps. The key novelty is to concentrate the difficult interactions at the nest level while retaining convex optimization over individual products, without discretizing prices or approximating demand. This structure makes the number of nests, rather than products, govern the exponent in a conditional worst-case complexity bound. The method returns feasible prices together with a bound on how much profit could still be gained, allowing decision makers to assess solution quality even when computation stops early. Extensions cover purchase-probability bounds and price-order rules, with explicit accounts of their computational cost. In synthetic experiments, the method certifies solutions for assortments of up to 500 products with few nests. Projecting unconstrained prices onto the feasible set loses up to 32.60% of profit relative to direct constrained optimization, highlighting the value of jointly optimizing substitution and feasibility.

item.title: Resolvent-Diagonal Energy of Isospectral Jacobi Matrices
item.description: We study the minimum squared resolvent diagonal among Jacobi matrices with prescribed eigenvalues. For the zeros of $P_n^{(α,β)}$, we construct a canonical realization and bound its asymptotic cost against the optimum. Its rescaled inverse converges to the Green operator of a reflection-symmetric singular Schrödinger operator with Bessel-zero spectrum. A Green-coordinate identity places this construction and all finite realizations in the same density framework. Mass-constrained spectral problems then give computable lower bounds. The bounds meet at $α=1/2$, with optimal energy $2/15$, and have first-order contact with derivative $-13/75$. We classify the constrained extremal profiles and the three endpoint geometries of the canonical density. Two polynomial families with the same limiting edge spectrum have different limiting optimal energies. For Nesterov momentum $(s-1)/(s+1)$, the optimal leading endpoint Hessian-drift gain among nonnegative-link Jacobi realizations is $\sqrt{2}$ times the original gain. An explicit isospectral flow strictly improves the standard one-sided realization for $α>-1/2$, $α\ne1/2$.

item.title: Fair Selection of Generalized Nash Equilibria: A Comparability Perspective
item.description: Generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problems model self-interested agents coupled through their costs and shared constraints, and arise throughout control applications that allocate a scarce common resource. Such problems typically admit a continuum of equilibria, so any implementation must \emph{select} one. This selection is not neutral: it decides how the cost of the shared constraint is distributed among the agents, a decision often expected to be fair. The variational GNE (v-GNE), which charges all agents a uniform shadow price, is the conventional choice and is frequently advocated as fair. Through the lens of \emph{comparability} from social choice theory, we show that the GNE set itself requires no inter-agent comparability of costs, whereas the v-GNE implicitly assumes cardinal unit comparability, one of the stronger notions. We then introduce the fair GNE (f-GNE), which selects an equilibrium by explicitly optimizing a fairness metric matched to the comparability at hand, and give constructive routes to compute it for single-constraint and linear-quadratic games. An electric-vehicle charging game serves as a running example throughout this self-contained tutorial.

item.title: A Smooth Equality Reformulation of Nonlinear Exponential Cone Optimization
item.description: Exponential cone optimization has received considerable attention in the modern literature, but studies involving nonlinear objective and constraint functions are still limited. This work can be seen as one of the first steps toward understanding nonlinear exponential cone optimization (NECO) problems. Here, we ask the question "Can smooth equality constraints replace nonlinear exponential cone constraints?". From a practical point of view, even squared slack reformulations in nonlinear programming introduce difficulties. However, such reformulations can be useful for studying optimality conditions. Motivated by this observation, in this work, we use a smooth surjective parameterization of the exponential cone to reformulate NECO as an equality-constrained nonlinear program (RNLP). We then analyze Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) and second-order optimality conditions for NECO through RNLP. Although feasibility is represented exactly, the KKT conditions for RNLP do not in general guarantee those for NECO. We characterize this correspondence through multiplier restrictions that are equivalent to a second-order condition involving only slack variables. We also establish an exact curvature identity showing that RNLP reproduces the sigma term of NECO without additional assumptions. Finally, we prove the relationships between second-order necessary and sufficient conditions for the two problems. We identify when RNLP can be used to rule out local minimizers of NECO or establish strict local optimality for NECO without explicitly evaluating the sigma term.

item.title: Maximizing Reaction via Spatial Localization: The Reaction-Flux Landscape and Maximizing Sequences
item.description: We continue our study of a PDE-constrained variational model for maximizing the total reaction flux by optimizing the spatial distribution of catalytic materials, such as enzymes. The total amount of enzyme is fixed, and the substrate concentration is governed by a reaction-diffusion equation with prescribed boundary values. We consider both linear and nonlinear Michaelis-Menten reaction kinetics. In previous work, we constructed a maximizing sequence, computed the first and second variations of the reaction functional, and established the nonexistence of local maximizers. Here, we conduct a more comprehensive analysis. We prove that the functional is strictly concave for linear kinetics but need not be concave or convex for nonlinear kinetics. We also show that no critical points exist. We then characterize maximizing sequences and identify all their possible limiting measures. Our analysis reveals the mechanism of reaction maximization through spatial localization: maximizing sequences concentrate enzymes near the portion of the boundary where the substrate concentration is largest. Moreover, the landscape of the functional defining the total reaction differs between the linear and nonlinear cases, a point less emphasized in applications. Consistent with existing biophysical studies, these findings motivate the development and analysis of regularized models.

item.title: Second-order optimality conditions for $C^{1,1}$ sparsity constrained optimization problems via disjunctive programming
item.description: In this paper, we investigate second-order necessary and sufficient optimality conditions for a class of $C^{1,1}$ sparsity constrained optimization problems via a disjunctive programming approach. More precisely, by utilizing the limiting/Mordukhovich second-order subdifferential of the associated Lagrangian function, we establish new second-order necessary and sufficient optimality conditions for local optimal solutions. These results are derived under mild assumptions and extend several existing results in the literature. In addition, we apply our theoretical developments to sparse multiobjective optimization problems and derive second-order optimality conditions for efficient solutions.

item.title: The multiplier step size in classical two-block ADMM: convergence and counterexamples
item.description: How large can the multiplier step be in the classical two-block alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM)? We keep the penalty fixed and use the usual primal updates. We consider finite-dimensional problems with closed proper convex objectives. We assume that a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker point exists and that each block subproblem attains its minimum at every step. Under these assumptions, the constraint images and the multiplier converge for a range of factors that extends beyond the golden ratio. The constraint matrices may be rank deficient. For larger steps, we construct two fixed compact polytopes and give an explicit threshold below two. The polytopes admit an infeasible periodic orbit for every factor at or above this threshold. At that threshold, ADMM can cycle even for smooth strongly convex objectives. This gives a negative answer to Glowinski's question about the full interval from zero to two. A different pair of piecewise-quadratic objectives gives geometrically growing residuals. For the general convex class, we locate the endpoint of the uniform convergence interval near 1.88688256. A convergence certificate on the unit circle gives the lower bound, while a separate periodic orbit gives the upper bound. Exact arithmetic verifies that the two bounds differ by less than 0.000000174.

item.title: Real-Time Nonlinear Mixed-Integer Model Predictive Control With Horizon-Tail Relaxations
item.description: Model predictive control (MPC) of nonlinear systems with discrete decisions leads to mixed-integer nonlinear programs (MINLPs) whose combinatorial complexity often prevents real-time deployment. In this paper, we propose a decomposition-based MPC method that reorders and reduces computations to shorten the delay between receiving a state measurement and applying the control input. Before the measurement arrives, we solve a continuous relaxation of the MINLP at a predicted state and construct a mixed-integer quadratic program (MIQP). Once the measured state is available, we solve the MIQP that reconstructs the discrete controls and simultaneously performs one sequential quadratic programming step toward the corresponding nonlinear solution. To reduce the combinatorial complexity in the horizon length, we either fix the integer controls or relax their integrality over the prediction horizon tail, while retaining an integer-feasible first control input. We derive error bounds relating the nonlinear objective values obtained with the horizon-tail approximations to the optimal value of the original mixed-integer problem. In a data center cooling example, the proposed method reduces mean feedback computation time by 94% relative to a state-of-the-art MINLP method with a total closed-loop cost difference of less than 1%.

item.title: Controlled Excitation for Identification of Nonlinear Systems with Saturated Outputs
item.description: We consider nonlinear systems whose measured output is the product of an unknown matrix and a known saturation function of the unmeasured state. Generating excitation that allows the matrix to be recovered from the output is challenging when the dynamics are largely unknown. We exploit saturation to construct this excitation. Under a geometric accessibility condition, we derive explicit open-loop controls that drive the state into regions where the saturation takes prescribed values. For componentwise saturations, this condition holds generically with as few as two independent control directions. The controls require no state measurement and only partial knowledge of the dynamics, with no information on the structure of its nonlinear part. The resulting regressor is known in advance, and the unknown matrix is recovered exactly by a closed-form regression. Under stronger structural assumptions and with sufficiently many independent outputs, an output feedback tracks prescribed reference trajectories within the unsaturated region to arbitrary accuracy and permits exact state recovery. Suitably chosen references then also enable exact identification of linearly parameterized (nonlinear) dynamics. We analyze robustness to measurement noise and illustrate the method numerically in the presence of both measurement and dynamical noise.

item.title: Provable State Estimation with Recurrent Models
item.description: Estimating the state of a dynamical system from observations is a crucial task in robotics and control. Despite their empirical success, recurrent models often lack formal guarantees on convergence and robustness. We bridge this gap by analyzing these architectures from the perspective of nonlinear observer theory. By framing RNNs as a time-discretization of continuous latent dynamical systems (Neural ODEs), we demonstrate that enforcing a contraction condition on the latent flow guarantees the existence of a smooth, injective map of the true physical state into the latent space. We prove that this architecture acts as a tunable observer: by increasing a single scalar gain that scales the latent vector field, the estimation error can be driven to an arbitrarily small neighborhood of zero at an exponentially fast rate. We further establish quantitative bounds on the MLP complexity required to decode this latent state, and extend our formal guarantees to the discrete-time residual RNN implementation. We validate the theory on a real mobile robotic task, where a provably contracting model outperforms a vanilla GRU with substantially more stable training. We also report that unconstrained GRUs converge to contracting dynamics on this task, suggesting that contraction is an emergent property of well-trained sequence models.

item.title: Tracking of a Moving Target on a Hyperboloid and its Extension to Leader-follower Formation Controller
item.description: This paper proposes a novel controller for a double-integrator agent to track a moving target with bounded velocity on a hyperboloid $\mathbb{H}^n$. The control law uses the intrinsic Riemannian structure of the hyperboloid, including the logarithm map, covariant derivative, and parallel transport, to make all its terms coordinate-free. Such formulation eases the implementation of the proposed tracking controller in the ambient Minkowski space without doing any additional chart computations. We use Barbalat's lemma for the hyperboloid to establish the convergence proof. Later, the proposed tracking controller is extended to a leader-follower formation control, where each agent reaches at a desired position around a moving leader in $\mathbb{H}^n$. We validate the results with numerical simulations considering two different target trajectories, geodesic and spiral, as examples.

item.title: Hierarchical Signal Temporal Logic Control of Continuous-Time Systems
item.description: For linear continuous-time systems, we solve the signal temporal logic (STL) control problem by translating it from continuous to discrete time such that a solution to the discrete-time problem guarantees a solution to the original continuous-time one. We split control synthesis into three hierarchical tasks. First, we discretize the continuous-time STL formula into a discrete-time one by sampling the temporal behavior it specifies. We accordingly discretize the continuous-time system by constructing a discrete-time model such that the input-state trajectories of the continuous-time system can be characterized as piecewise polynomial interpolations of the input-state trajectories of the discrete-time model. Second, we exploit this characterization to formulate mixed-integer linear constraints on the discrete-time trajectories that allow for planning a trajectory whose piecewise polynomial interpolation satisfies the continuous-time STL formula. In fact, system discretization and trajectory planning are performed in such a manner that any feasible solution to these constraints gives a discrete-time trajectory that can be transformed into a continuous-time one guaranteed to satisfy the original STL formula. Third, we propose a step-by-step algorithm to construct the control input that realizes such continuous-time trajectory.

item.title: PH-Symb : Sparse symbolic identification of nonlinear port-Hamiltoniansystems using Kolmogorov-Arnold networks
item.description: The paper introduces PH-Symb, a novel symbolic structure-preserving identification method, that combines Kolmogorov Arnold networks and sparse regression to build explicit port-Hamiltonian (pH) models from data. Unlike other Machine Learning or neural pH approaches, PH-Symb recovers physically interpretable and explicit-symbolic components and enforces pH structure by construction. It also introduces a new normalization method that preserves the pH structure. It allows handling both identification from input-state-output (ISO) data and input-output (IO) data, and applications show it delivers interpretable models and lower errors than neural baselines on synthetic and real-world systems.

item.title: Approximation Algorithms for Right-Hand-Side Parametric Linear Programming Problems
item.description: In parametric linear optimization problems, the objective function or the feasible set depends linearly on one or several real-valued parameters. The goal is to provide an optimal solution set, i.e., a set containing an optimal solution for each non-parametric problem induced by a particular choice of parameter values. In this paper, we consider right-hand-side single-parametric linear programming problems (RHS-PLPPs) that are usually very difficult to solve exactly. An optimal solution set of minimum cardinality can be infinite, while a representation by optimal bases may still require super-polynomially many different bases. Hence, we develop approximation methods for RHS-PLPPs that compute approximation sets of polynomially bounded cardinality, each containing, for every parameter value, a feasible solution whose objective value is at most a prescribed multiplicative factor times the optimum. Our first approach constructs an approximation set using a greedy staircase procedure and yields an FPTAS under general sufficient conditions. We show that these conditions hold for some important classes of RHS-PLPPs. For monotone instances, in which the feasible sets are nested as the parameter varies, our algorithm yields an approximation set of minimum cardinality. Beyond monotonicity, we establish near-minimum cardinality guarantees under more general sufficient conditions. Finally, we introduce a dual approximation algorithm that returns solutions with objective value no greater than the optimum while allowing a controlled multiplicative violation of the parameter-dependent right-hand sides.

item.title: Improved Approximation and Hardness Bounds for $β$-TSP
item.description: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) asks for a minimum-length Hamiltonian cycle in a complete weighted graph. Its approximability depends on the edge lengths: unrestricted instances admit no constant-factor approximation unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, metric instances admit Christofides' $3/2$-approximation, and fixed-dimensional Euclidean instances admit a PTAS. We study $β$-TSP, where the edge lengths satisfy $ \ell_{uw}\leqβ(\ell_{uv}+\ell_{vw}) \qquad \forall\,u,v,w\in V\ \text{pairwise distinct}, \quad β\in\left[\tfrac{1}{2},1\right]. $ The condition arises naturally in various settings, for example, when metric travel times are combined with positive service times at the vertices. The previous best approximation algorithm, due to Böckenhauer et al., ranges from $1$ at $β=1/2$ to $3/2$ as $β$ approaches $1$. We obtain a strictly better guarantee for every $1/2<β<1$ by combining two simple constructions whose guarantees counterbalance each other. We also improve the best known approximation hardness bound for every $1/2<β<1$.

item.title: The BCC lattice is the optimal 3D lattice quantizer for all $p\geq1$
item.description: For every finite $p\ge1$, the body-centered cubic lattice uniquely minimizes the $p$th moment of the Voronoi cell among three-dimensional lattices of covolume one, up to orthogonal transformations. This proves the Graf--Luschgy conjecture for three-dimensional lattice quantizers (\cite{GL}).

item.title: Data-driven representation of continuous-time linear time-invariant behaviors via Hankel integral operators
item.description: We present a data-driven representation of the finite-horizon behavior of deterministic controllable continuous-time LTI systems. We first introduce a notion of persistency of excitation for continuous-time signals that does not require the signal to be differentiable. We then show that, when the input is persistently exciting in this sense, the closure of the range of a Hankel integral operator built from a single input-output trajectory equals the behavior of the system over a finite time horizon. This result provides a nonparametric representation of system trajectories directly in terms of measured data, without requiring an explicit parametric model of the system.

item.title: Can a Language Model Write the Weights? An Empirical Study of LLM-Written Scoring Networks for Column Generation and MILP Branching, with a Bus-Driver Scheduling Application
item.description: This paper was generated by an AI model (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) under the author's direction; all results come from computations run on the author's machine, and every reference was checked. Weight-space programming (WSP) is the idea that a large language model (LLM) can write the weights of a small neural network directly, guided only by reading forward-pass outputs, with no gradient training. We test whether WSP can improve exact operations research algorithms where they rely on cheap scoring rules. In four studies, an LLM wrote small multilayer perceptrons that (i) select arcs, labels and ng-neighbourhoods inside column generation for the vehicle routing problem with time windows, and (ii) choose branching variables in SCIP's branch-and-bound. The algorithms stay exact whatever the weights; a bad network only costs time. In column generation, no lever gave a material gain. In branching on synthetic classes, a hand-written network solved independent-set instances in 0.37x the time of SCIP's default rule (18 paired instances, Wilcoxon $p<10^{-5}$) and matched or beat networks trained by imitation of strong branching, but on 39 MIPLIB 2017 instances it solved 19 versus 24. In an application built from the real GTFS feed of Atlanta's transit agency (MARTA), a crew scheduling set-partitioning model solved by a native C plugin with SCIP's factory settings, the LLM-written rules took 0.63x the default's time on 32 held-out instances ($p<10^{-4}$), but SCIP's plain pseudocost rule did exactly as well (ratio 0.99, $p=0.19$). In these settings, the gains came from being cheap, not from what the LLM wrote. All code, logs and the numbers behind every figure are released.

item.title: Solver-Free Decision-Focused Learning via Neural Optimization Layers for Edge Selection
item.description: Decision-focused learning trains prediction models to improve downstream decisions, but many methods require costly solver calls or optimal-solution labels. We propose a solver-free decision-focused learning framework for NP-hard edge-selection problems with uncertain parameters in the objective, the constraints, or both. A neural optimization layer is first trained without solution labels, using problem objectives and constraint penalties. Graph-informed edge scoring and iterative refinement encourage concentrated and structurally consistent continuous decisions. The layer is then frozen, and a prediction model is trained through its continuous output using a problem-specific loss evaluated under observed parameters. At deployment, the predictor, optimization layer, and a lightweight decoder produce decisions without solving the original NP-hard problem. Experiments on the asymmetric traveling salesperson and endpoint-free orienteering problems show consistently better decision quality than prediction-focused learning and improvements over most evaluated decision-focused baselines. Our framework requires less training time than the evaluated decision-focused baselines, even when optimization-layer pretraining is included. Neural deployment also produces decisions faster than solver-based deployment, offering a better quality-efficiency trade-off. The layer also reduces training cost in existing decision-focused methods when used as an approximate optimization oracle.

item.title: A Regular First-Order Calculus for the Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao Geometry
item.description: We introduce a notion of intrinsic differentiability for functionals on the space of finite nonnegative measures equipped with the Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao (WFR) distance, also known as the Hellinger--Kantorovich (HK) distance. The resulting static first-order calculus accounts simultaneously for spatial transport and mass reweighting. We characterize regular barycentric logarithms through optimal semicouplings and measurable selections at the transport threshold, and prove their tangency at arbitrary finite source measures. The defining expansion extends to non-optimal semicouplings, with remainder of smaller order than the square root of their cost. This yields differentiation formulas for simultaneous transport and reweighting and uniqueness of the gradients. We also give a sufficient criterion in terms of regular flat derivatives. We characterize differentiability of one half the squared WFR distance by a common optimal Monge transport--growth representation with no target mass created from the cone vertex. Equivalently, the regular barycentric logarithm is unique and its norm equals the distance; the gradient is minus this logarithm. Finally, we formulate the corresponding calculus on probability measures. On $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, WFR differentiability implies intrinsic Wasserstein differentiability, with the transport component of the WFR gradient coinciding with the Wasserstein gradient. Whenever a flat derivative exists, one quarter of the reaction component agrees almost everywhere with its centered representative. As a byproduct we obtain a Wasserstein differentiability result for the squared $\mathrm{WFR}$ distance.

item.title: Row-sparse ah-symmetric reflexive generalized inverses with a few extra rows: local search with approximation guarantees
item.description: For a rank-$r$ matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, ah-symmetric reflexive generalized inverses $H$ with few nonzero rows give least-squares solutions that are fast to evaluate and use few variables. A known determinant-based local search finds one with exactly $r$ nonzero rows and 2,1-norm within an essentially tight factor $r$ of the minimum at an exact local optimum. We let the nonzero rows of $H$ lie in a set $K$ of $k\ge r$ indices and study how to choose $K$. We bound the loss of this restriction (restricted over unrestricted minimum 2,1-norm) by a simple geometric certificate and establish that a local search maximizing the squared rank-$r$ volume of the corresponding columns of $A$ gives loss at most $\sqrt{k(r+εk)/(k-r+1)}$, where $1+ε$ is the swap tolerance. With $ε=0$ this is $r$ at $k=r$ and less than $\sqrt{2r}$ for $k\ge2r$; with $ε=1/k$ the search runs in polynomial time on rational data. The same support yields an ah-symmetric reflexive generalized inverse with spectral norm within a factor $\sqrt{1+(n-k)(r+εk)/(k-r+1)}$ of that of the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. The loss guarantees hold for every norm on the rows. In general, our certificate bound is tight up to a factor depending only on $k/r$, and on some instances, for a suitable row norm, so is the loss bound; for the 2,1-norm, however, the certificate can overestimate the loss by a factor $\sqrt r$. The local search is the Fedorov exchange algorithm of 0/1 D-optimal design; this yields a fast implementation and, via the Kiefer-Wolfowitz theorem, supports of at most $r(r+1)/2+1$ rows with certificate at most $\sqrt r$, best possible in general. On instances from earlier work, the observed loss is far below the guarantee, and the method matches two ADMM heuristics when few rows are removed and otherwise gives 2,1-norms up to 27% smaller, one to two orders of magnitude faster.

item.title: Fixed-point acceleration on Neural Wasserstein manifolds
item.description: We propose a fixed-point acceleration method for optimization over probability measures, applicable to a variety of machine learning problems. We represent probability measures as pushforwards of a reference distribution through a neural network map and equip the parameter space with the induced pullback Wasserstein metric. This geometric structure allows natural gradient descent to be interpreted as a fixed-point iteration on a Riemannian manifold. We accelerate this iteration using Riemannian Anderson mixing method, which exploits historical residuals to capture approximate second-order information without forming Hessians. In the present parametric setting, the manifold is represented by Euclidean coordinates endowed with a point-dependent metric, simplifying retraction and vector transport. We evaluate the method on multimodal sampling, PDE-based inverse problems, aggregation dynamics, Bayesian logistic regression, and generative modeling. Across the tested tasks, Anderson mixing reduces the number of natural-gradient iterations and achieves competitive performance relative to SGD and Adam in terms of both loss-gradient evaluations and wall-clock time. These results suggest that fixed-point acceleration is an efficient tool for improving the computational efficiency of training on parametric Wasserstein methods.

item.title: Attractivity Implies Lyapunov Stability for Multidimensional Fornasini--Marchesini Systems
item.description: We study the linear multidimensional Fornasini--Marchesini recurrence with uniformly bounded boundary data prescribed on the open coordinate faces. Attractivity is understood in the sense of Pringsheim convergence, in which all discrete indices tend to infinity. We establish that attractivity alone implies Lyapunov stability, and consequently is equivalent to asymptotic stability, for an arbitrary number of discrete directions. Our proof combines inheritance of attractivity by lower-dimensional subsystems, a Baire-category uniform boundedness argument, and word-sum estimates to control coordinate slabs outside the Pringsheim tail. We use a generalized spectral stability criterion proved in a separate companion preprint, without reproving that criterion here. We also obtain a uniform exponential interior estimate and contrast our boundary/convergence convention with an earlier two-dimensional attractivity theorem.

item.title: Quasipolynomial-Time Planning for Decodable POMDPs
item.description: We study planning for finite-horizon partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) with finite state, action, and observation spaces. Both exact and approximate planning are known to be computationally hard in this setting, so prior work has explored natural assumptions that make planning easier. Recent work [Golowich et al., 2022] gave quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for observable POMDPs. These are POMDPs whose observation channels satisfy an $\ell_1$-observability condition, but notably, no assumptions are required on the transition dynamics. In a similar vein, for every fixed $ρ>0$, we give quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for $ρ$-decodable POMDPs. We show that decodability is implied by both $\ell_1$- and $\ell_2$-observability and is strictly weaker than observability. Moreover, we show that the optimal decodability constant can be computed in polynomial time, whereas computing the optimal $\ell_1$-observability constant is NP-hard in the worst case. We also show that the fast filter-forgetting guarantee underlying the approach of [Golowich et al., 2022] does not extend directly from $\ell_1$-observability to constant $\ell_2$-observability. Thus, decodability is an easy-to-check, unifying assumption under which quasipolynomial-time approximate planning for POMDPs is possible.

item.title: Instantaneous control for stabilization of interacting particle systems: convergence rates and dominant frequencies
item.description: We study a class of Cucker-Smale-type systems with a binary interaction potential subject to an external control input. We apply an instantaneous rolling horizon control (IRHC) feedback to address two different control problems: full set-point stabilization of a spatial configuration with zero velocity and stabilization of the center of mass at a desired position with zero mean velocity using a single external agent. The IRHC feedback has been shown to preserve the port-Hamiltonian structure of the corresponding open-loop systems. We analyze how the control parameters and the time discretization affect convergence rates and oscillation frequencies and compare the IRHC feedback with the corresponding IDA-PBC feedback obtained by omitting an additional correction term. For the reduced center of mass dynamics, we derive explicit predictions for continuous- and discrete-time spectral decay rates and oscillation frequencies and verify these predictions numerically. For the full nonlinear particle system, the controller comparison is done by numerical experiments.

item.title: Geometric Pairwise Classification of Affine Constraints over Ellipsoidal Regions
item.description: This paper presents a deterministic geometric procedure for analysing affine constraints over fixed ellipsoidal regions, motivated by chance-constrained set approximation. Analytical tests classify inequalities as always violated, never violated, or cutting. Pairwise tests determine whether two inequalities can be strictly violated at a common point, yielding a compatibility matrix. The tests follow from quadratic optimisation and the Karush--Kuhn--Tucker conditions, with explicit treatment of tangencies, parallel normals, and degenerate inequalities. The formulation applies in arbitrary finite dimensions and provides geometric information for subsequent bounds on simultaneous sampled violations and safe-region approximation.

item.title: On the (non-)closedness of the set of ReLU networks
item.description: We prove that the set $\mathcal{N}_N$ of ReLU networks with one hidden layer and at most $N\in\mathbb N$ neurons is weakly closed in $W^{1,p}(Ω)$, for a bounded connected open set $Ω\subset\mathbb R^d$. Consequently, every coercive, weakly lower semicontinuous energy on this space attains its minimum over $\mathcal{N}_N$. This covers the Deep Ritz method with convex integrands, Sobolev training and Lipschitz learning. Moreover, as the weight decay parameter tends to zero, minimizers of the regularized problem converge, up to subsequences, to minimizers with minimal parameter norm. We also prove that the set of ReLU networks with two hidden layers of bounded widths is not closed in $W^{1,p}(Ω)$ or in $C(\overlineΩ)$. This disproves a conjecture of Petersen, Raslan and Voigtlaender.
